records.title: Show HN: Pulse Local, a Mac budgeting app whose AI models run on your machine
records.author: niztk
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm Niz. Pulse Local is a budgeting app for Mac (Apple Silicon, beta) that answers questions about your spending with models that run on your machine. Local mode needs no account. The ledger and your questions stay on the machine, and the app sends no analytics or crash logs.

I felt there are not enough consumer apps that run locally with no calls to the outside world that help us manage sensitive corners of our lives. This app in its local variant only downloads a couple of models and occasional updates, it does not send any analytics nor data.

Features-wise, Pulse local is a complete budgeting app that offers an assistant built on top of a fine-tuned model and thousands of rules embedded in the code itself. I'm sharing it for free with options to help me continue experimenting with fine-tuning and expanding along this direction.

How it works: you import a CSV from any bank, in any currency. When you ask a question, a tuned Qwen3 0.6B model reads it into a structured query, and code, not the model, does the money math against the ledger. A 4B checker model double-checks each money answer; when the two readings disagree, the app says it is not sure instead of guessing. That change took wrong answers from about one in five to 5 in 494 questions across our last three tests. The write-up covers how we test, the designs that failed, and the limits of the claim: https://pulseos.finance/pulse-local/writing/agree-or-not-sur...

The tuned weights are on Hugging Face (PulseOS/pulse-local-qwen3-0.6b).

Limitations: the first start downloads about 2.9 GB of models. With the checker on, a money answer takes 12 to 14 seconds (you can turn the checker off). Small models can still misread an open-ended question. The app answers in English. Mac only for now; Windows is next.

The app is free. An optional Connected mode (Sync Pass, $29/year) syncs US banks through Plaid; transactions pass through our server's memory and are not stored.

Feedback welcome, especially on wrong answers and on questions it should handle but does not.

records.title: Show HN: Parsimony – an open-source benchmark for how much code AI models add
records.author: lasu
records.storyText:
Existing benchmarks measure solve rate and token output/cost, but don't punish excess code, which makes a codebase harder to work with in the long term. I wanted to measure this since it matters most for long-term projects.

Method: it takes the patches that benchmarks already publish (DeepSWE, SWE-bench Verified, SWE-bench Live) and counts "coding units": syntax elements like statements, calls, names and literals. I didn't use lines of code, so cramming code isn't rewarded. Deleted code is subtracted, so it measures net units.

GPT-6 and Claude 5.5 have no public patches yet, so I ran them myself on 3–10 tasks on my own subscriptions (shown as faded circles, not ranked).

Any feedback or model contributions are welcome, especially public patch exports for newer models.

GitHub: https://github.com/La5u/Parsimony

Not affiliated with any of the benchmarks.

records.title: Show HN: T0: We trained a 256M SOTA open-weights time-series forecasting model
records.author: LTMeyer
records.storyText:
Hi everyone, we are excited to share t0-gamma, the latest model in our t0 family. It is a 256M parameter open-weights foundation model for time series (TSFM). It runs on CPU, GPU or Apple chips.

https://huggingface.co/theforecastingcompany/t0-gamma

t0 leverages historical data to forecast the likely outcomes over a given horizon. It does so zero-shot. It works on almost any time series, as it can pick up small signals like trends and seasonality. It can also leverage future-known information, like holidays, promotions and weather forecasts. Under the hood, t0 is a transformer that alternates attention between time and across the variates of a series.

t0 is agnostic to the domain and to the frequency of the time series. For instance, it can be used to predict retail or electricity demand, as well as server metrics.

On European day ahead electricity prices, t0 reduces the error by a third compared with a naive baseline that repeats the previous day. Adding weather forecasts or holiday information improves it even further. There is a Colab notebook to try it. t0 has also been tested independently on electricity prices in Texas (ERCOT).

https://colab.research.google.com/github/theforecastingcompa...

Like other TSFMs, t0 outperforms classical techniques such as ARIMA, ETS and their variants. On the public benchmarks GIFT-Eval, fev-bench and TIME, t0-gamma currently ranks first among the other TSFMs. It means it is the most accurate model there is to date. Like other TSFMs, t0 can be used inside agentic, routing or ensembling systems. This can improve the scores on the leaderboards even further. Our tech report describes the model family and its evaluation.

https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.24559

Trying it takes a few Python lines.

  pip install "tfc-t0[torch]>=0.6.0"

  from t0 import T0Forecaster
  model = T0Forecaster.from_pretrained("theforecastingcompany/t0-gamma").eval()
  history = ...  # history of the time series to predict
  out = model.predict(history, horizon=24)
  out.median
There is more to come. We are working to extend t0 to joint forecasts across related series and hierarchies, much longer contexts and faster inference.

Please give it a try, and don't hesitate to tell us where it works and where it doesn't.

We are The Forecasting Company. We want to help companies reduce their uncertainty about the future, so they can make better decisions. We are starting our journey by building foundation models for time series.

records.title: Show HN: Treesum – Replace MS Excel/Project with a Code Editor
records.author: mallahan
records.storyText:
# Intro

The goal of this software is to make it easy to get the plan that's in your head onto the page. Start with the outline then add details. Then more details. Then numbers: costs, time, quantities. Then organize and categorize with #tags. All the sums, graphs and pivot table functionality happens automatically in the Calcs, Timeline, Stats views. And everything looks nice without you having to format it.

Currently, it's all local, saved in your browser. Save your plan permanently by downloading the '.tsum' file. Open (upload) the '.tsum' to start working again. Everything happens in the browser. The files are stored where ever you like. The '.tsum' file is just text - human and AI readable. Use it to plan anything. We hope it works like your brain does - by organizing things in trees.

# Story

This software is entirely vibe-coded. It had to be - none of my developer friends would help me out. The front end JS on this app is too complex for a part time developer like myself. I've had this idea for a while and was only able to bring it to life because of AI. It may not gain traction, but at least I can put it out there, use it myself, or stop thinking about it altogether. It's amazing to see it and actually use it - to know if my idea was good or not, at least for me. And I'm actually happy with it and have been using it. If you have thoughts about the idea, feel free to let me know. I'm open to suggestions for improvement.

# Disclaimer

This tool is mainly intended to help with project planning. But it can be used for any data that looks more like a tree than a table. Creating a quote or estimate for one-off projects is my favorite use case. The varying structure of costs across lumber, electrical, concrete and labor fits well.

Obviously, it doesn't replace all the many things Excel can do. It tries to improve on MS Project by making it easier to get your schedule on the page by coding into an editor instead of poking at menus in a GUI. It is still a proof of concept at this point, not a bullet-proof software package. If there's interest, it will be developed further. For now, it's good enough for me.

# Roadmap

I want this software to be the Excalidraw of Excel: free, simple, browser-based and fun to use. There are great things that Excalidraw does that would require servers and more costs. These features could be turned into a paid product if there is interest. So, if you're interested, please let me know: treesum.app (at) gmail.com.

# Thanks HN

This project would not have been possible with out AI. But also not without HN. Reading HN nearly every work day really shapes how to think about software and presenting it to people - especially for someone who is not a full-time developer. It's a great community and I've happily been a member since (at least) 2013.

records.title: Show HN: Hatoba, an open-source SSH client with an AI assistant and E2EE sync
records.author: scarletkc
records.storyText:
I've used SSH tools for years and didn't really plan on building yet another SSH client, but I ended up building one the way I wanted. Hatoba is a desktop SSH client for Windows, Linux and macOS. It's written in Rust with Tauri 2 and MIT licensed.

Each terminal has an AI assistant panel next to it. You describe the problem, and it reads the terminal screen, runs commands, types into the shell, and reads, edits and searches files on the host to find the cause and fix it. You can approve every command and edit it before it runs, let a model you pick approve the safe ones, or turn approval off. Files it changes show a diff you can undo. It works with any OpenAI-compatible or Anthropic API, local models included, and supports skills and MCP servers.

Sync doesn't go through a server of mine. Hatoba deploys a Worker and a D1 database to your own Cloudflare account and syncs hosts, keys and AI conversations through them. The free plan usually covers personal use. Everything is encrypted on the device before it leaves. Keys are derived from your master password with Argon2id, every item is encrypted with AES-256-GCM, and the Worker only stores ciphertext plus the hashes it needs to sign you in. Someone who gets hold of the whole Cloudflare account still only gets ciphertext. Sync is optional, and everything works offline without it.

The usual SSH client features are there too: groups, tags and fuzzy search, ~/.ssh/config import, ProxyJump and SOCKS5/HTTP proxies, an SFTP panel, local port forwarding, and a key vault that imports OpenSSH, PEM and PuTTY keys. There's also a dashboard showing CPU, memory, disk and network for every saved host, read over plain SSH with nothing installed on the servers. SSH is russh, the terminal is xterm.js with the WebGL renderer, and the UI is React.

I develop on Windows, so it's Windows first, with a custom title bar that supports Snap Layouts and Mica, and working CJK input methods. The Linux packages and the macOS build get far less testing on real machines. The macOS build is Apple Silicon only and isn't notarized, so macOS blocks it on first launch until you allow it in Privacy & Security. Bug reports from Linux and Mac users would help the most.

Website: https://hatoba.fog.moe Downloads: https://hatoba.fog.moe/download/

records.title: Show HN: What are vector embeddings? An interactive guide
records.author: afistfullof
records.storyText:
Hey HN, I'm Abdur-Rahman Butler, a machine learning engineer at Isaacus.

I made an interactive write-up that walks you through the A to Z of vector embeddings, inspired by Brendan Bycroft's incredible interactive LLM visualisation guide (see here - https://bbycroft.net/llm).

Most of my work is on encoder models, and I kept noticing how few good interactive resources there are on embeddings. The ones that do exist tend to either plot some embeddings in 3D or only explain a narrow applied technique like semantic search or RAG.

So I wanted to make something that teaches how embeddings work by letting you play with them. In the write-up, there are interactive visualisations that allow you to explore the concepts of vectorisation, cosine similarity, semantic search, hierarchical retrieval, clustering, zero-shot classification and deduplication.

The centrepiece of the post is a game I've dubbed 'SemanticGeussr'. It's inspired by Wordle and GeoGuessr, and the goal is to draw a loop around a random target word by triangulating guesses on a 2D map of 43,339 common English words.

It's admittedly a bit intimidating at first, as semantic space does not perfectly match our intuition of meaning. But once you get the hang of it, the game becomes really addictive. I recently had the pleasure of demoing the game to some law students at the University of Melbourne, and we had a lot of fun throwing different vector equations at it to see where they'd land.

Some fun ones to get started with:

  london - english + french
  running - land + water
  avg(breakfast, lunch, dinner)
  0.4 * noodles + 0.6 * pasta

records.title: Show HN: tsv has fast formatters and parsers for Svelte, TypeScript/JS, CSS
records.author: ryanatkn
records.storyText:
tsv is a set of performance-focused language tools for the Web. Today it ships formatters and parsers for TypeScript/JS, CSS, and Svelte, including a vscode/openvsx extension. JSON and HTML are planned, maybe linting after. The readme has a loose roadmap - https://github.com/fuzdev/tsv

tsv's benchmarks show how the Web's newer native tools have some performance left on the table. Formatting TypeScript, tsv is more than twice as fast as oxfmt, and is smaller and uses less memory - https://tsv.fuz.dev/docs/benchmarks

From the site:

- formatting TypeScript, tsv is ~2.2x faster than Oxfmt (native), ~36x faster than Prettier (native Rust vs Prettier's JS; ~26x as wasm), and ~7.6x faster than Biome (wasm)

- formatting Svelte, tsv is ~79x faster than Prettier (~55x as wasm) and ~10x faster than Biome (wasm)

- formatting CSS, tsv is ~3.6x faster than Oxfmt (native), ~111x faster than Prettier (~78x as wasm), and ~12x faster than Biome (wasm)

tsv is focused on the Web and Svelte, and doesn't support other nonstandard languages like JSX/TSX and SCSS. This limits possible adoption, but it keeps the tool slim and simple, and there are plenty of other tools that offer a generic language platform - tsv isn't trying to compete with them. Part of my motivation was being tired of slow tools and Svelte's second-class status in this next generation.

Before starting the project, I had tried to build on Oxc and Biome, and ran into some discouraging edges. On the benchmarks' language support section, you'll see Oxc doesn't export its CSS parser (recently added, a fork of Raffia - https://github.com/g-plane/raffia), and Biome doesn't export its parsers. Also oxfmt doesn't ship wasm to the browser yet, and tsv's smaller footprint is useful there (Biome is 46.9 MB to tsv's 2.7).

Parser conformance is as good or better than Oxc, Biome, and swc, except negative parser cases (errors), which are unfinished. https://tsv.fuz.dev/docs/conformance

The codebase turns 1 year old at the end of the month. It's my first serious AI-generated project, built with Claude Code. I learned Rust in 2015, built some toys including an arcade action prototype, and followed its development over the years, but this is my first project since. tsv wouldn't exist without LLMs - it requires far too much labor for a side project.

tsv leans heavily on Prettier, but doesn't copy it. This is why this production release took almost a year, despite the silly fast coding part. I made some different stylistic choices, more for Svelte than TypeScript, and fixed numerous quirks and bugs and documented them. tsv also takes advantage of Svelte 5's whitespace rules, which further diverged from HTML to trim leading whitespace in tags, fixing longstanding formatting warts - https://svelte.dev/docs/svelte/v5-migration-guide#Whitespace...

The formatter takes no style config, and instead is hardcoded to Prettier's style with Svelte's config. Supporting Prettier's config would force significant costs on tsv with a JS runtime, so instead I'm keeping the formatters non-configurable instead of making all users pay those costs. Part of these costs can be see in the CLI benchmark (which is a fork of Oxc's official bench-formatter) - when tsv's binary is used directly instead of via Node, the single-repo CLI benchmark runs tsv 1.7x faster using less than half the memory.

Next I'm exploring rearchitecting to Zig-inspired data-oriented parsing - https://mitchellh.com/zig/parser - which should get tsv closer to Yuku's speed, measured on the site.

The vscode extension is `fuzdev.tsv-format` - https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=fuzdev.t... - and Open VSX - https://open-vsx.org/extension/fuzdev/tsv-format

Repo: https://github.com/fuzdev/tsv

records.title: Show HN: PanamaKVM – direct-booting Linux from Java 25 via FFM/KVM
records.author: rusanoph
records.storyText:
Hi HN!

PanamaKVM is an experimental miniVM containing the bare minimum components needed to boot an x86 Linux kernel and run an interactive terminal. Its key feature is that it is built on top of Java 25 without using JNI. Instead, it utilizes the Foreign Function & Memory API (FFM).

I generally stick to Java LTS versions - having worked with Java 21 for a long time - so I recently decided to check if any new LTS releases had come out. It turns out I was a year late to the party regarding Java 25. While looking through the changelog, I noticed the new FFM for native code and decided to give it a try.

As it turned out, I was a couple of years late to the FFM feature :D, since it had already been introduced as a full-fledged part of the language in Java 22.

One interesting thing I discovered during implementation was a quirk in the ioctl ABI: there seemed to be a discrepancy between the KVM API documentation and the actual implementation. The very first call I attempted was KVM_GET_API_VERSION, but it unexpectedly returned EINVAL. After tracing the execution with strace, I managed to pinpoint the root cause (which was nearly impossible to debug at the Java level): the call was reaching the kernel without a third argument (whereas the documentation specified two). As it turns out, when the KVM documentation says an ioctl takes no arguments, it actually does require one... Due to KVM's implementation details, it implicitly expects a third parameter - it just has to be zero. This is likely to prevent reading garbage data from memory. Perhaps some readers have insights into the underlying reason for this difference - or maybe it was just human error and "things just turned out that way."

In any case, by following the instructions in the repository's README, you can boot a functional Linux kernel and interact with it via the terminal. I’ve only tested the launch using Alpine 3.24.2 x86-64 on WSL2, so that might be a limitation. However, if you run it on a different setup or on bare-metal Linux, that would be great - please let me know. And if something breaks in the process - even better - let me know about that too.

As for what I haven't finished yet in the current virtual machine implementation: networking and persistent storage are missing, and there is no virtio integration. Multi-vCPU startup mode isn't supported either; essentially, the creation of a single vCPU is currently hardcoded.

I’d also love to hear your thoughts on the project. I would particularly value any feedback regarding the use of FFM and the KVM API itself.

I’ll be happy to answer any questions you have.

When someone mentions Merlin in a Slack thread or Linear issue comment, the task runs on that team member's machine, using their own Claude Code or Codex runtime, and progress and results come back to the original thread. Teammates can steer the agent mid-run. Merlin also has schedules, shared skills, and memory.

I know you've probably heard about Claude Tag. Merlin is similar to that but also different. The model usage goes to the Claude Code or Codex subscription instead of API bill, and you can use Merlin across different surfaces to streamline workflow instead of just in Slack (Linear's agent session works particularly well with Merlin. You can just leverage Linear as your control panel for agentic work using Merlin). Merlin also runs on your local machines, which means that you can use your local context including MCPs, skills and local files instead of in a cloud sandbox.

Merlin does not upload your working directory, and provider credentials stay on the device. The request and the context it needs pass through Merlin. Runtimes start private, and an owner can make one public so teammates, including non-engineers, can use it.

But there're also some limits, and we'll probably deal with them in future updates: - An offline or sleeping machine can't take work. The same issue as OpenClaw. But if you have a mac mini or ec2 setup it should be fine. - Linux is CLI only. We may later add desktop for Linux. - While runtime delegation isn't a problem for now, we're still working on how to make the best use of each team member's local runtime and let them work together cohesively.

We've been internally using Merlin for quite some time. It really helps when you're trying to add some AI juice to the conversation or just delegate things to your agents. I think it reduces the friction of having to do the copying & pasting and switch to another app to ask for AI's input when you're having a discussion in a collaborative environment like Slack or Linear. It's really the fastest way from intent to execution.

Pricing: free for up to 5 active users and 1,000 requests/month. We think this should get small teams started and get real value from it. Team is $59/mo and Scale is $99/mo, with a 14-day Team trial and no credit card required.

records.title: Show HN: BScaff - A CLI tool for project scaffolding and snippets
records.author: akashnagcs
records.storyText:
I built BScaff, a CLI tool for saving and reusing project structures, templates, files, and text snippets. It can serve as a URL bookmark tool as well.

It started with project scaffolding, but I wanted something more general-purpose: a tool that could save almost any reusable starting point and bring it back whenever needed. For each language, I had a specific way of structuring projects that I have refined over years, but I could not find any tool which can quickly help to generate such scaffolding quickly. Copier and Cookiecutter exists but they depend on templates, and I didn't want to create templates for such tasks. One more use-case I had was when I used AI chatbots who suggest some project structure, and I want to quickly create that. So I wanted something offline which can quickly help me save and recreate file trees. Then I added snippets to it too, but I mostly use it for notes taking personally.

Some things you can do with it:

* Save Git repository templates locally and use them offline whenever you need to create a new project

* Create reusable templates from existing directories

* Save and recreate directory structures by copying ASCII file trees and the tool will read it from clipboard and recreate it (or save it for later)

* Save collections of files and generate them again in another directory

* Save text snippets and either copy them to the clipboard or generate files from them

The idea is to avoid repeatedly recreating the same boilerplate, directory structures, configuration files, etc. And you can use it as a note-taking app as well with snippets. It has templates support as well with Jinja-based variable replacement. Template updates are supported, but project updates are not yet implemented, have planned it for future.

It is written in TypeScript, runs on Node.js, and is available on npm.

GitHub: https://github.com/akashnag/bscaff

Install: npm install -g @akashnag/bscaff

Feedback, feature suggestions ( I already have a big backlog though :P ), and contributions are welcome!

records.title: Show HN: Codepill – New atomic licensing scheme
records.author: X-Ryl669
records.storyText:
Proposal specification: https://x-ryl669.github.io/codepill/

I've got frustrated of selecting the right licenses in many of my projects, because of the subtle differences in all of them and the large incompatibilities while mixing them. Also, I often find that some part of a document should be more restricted that the rest (think of a documentation you want in public domain citing GPLv3 code, or a GPLv3 code citing restricted standard text). Also, this scheme should be able to merge both "textual" licenses with "artistic" licenses like CC.

Hence I'm proposing a new scheme that clearly specifies what "rights" you're reserving for what part of a document, media, opus, speech. It's composable, it's simple to use for both humans and machine, it allows to deny machine processing (under the jurisdictions that do protect citizens against those).

I'm asking for feedback for this idea, is there something that you'd like to protect that I've forgotten, or do you find it convenient to use and understand ?

Hi Hacker News! I'm Tim, and I made y'all some Pasta. :)

My favorite catch so far: I asked for a 500 kg deadlift for 100 reps, and the model built it, no questions asked. I'm hoping to make the evals better as I get more feedback on what's working and what's not. Over time, I'd like it to come as close as possible to what a certified personal trainer would build for you based on your goals and needs.

I also realize that getting fit and working out isn't solely about knowing what to do. There's also the motivation + accountability part, and I do have some ideas on the roadmap that I'll share later. And I swear, it's not gamifying your health and fitness results.

You'll need an iPhone with Apple Intelligence on iOS 27, and it's free for 7 days. Give it a try. I'd love to know what you ask it for first, and whether you'd do the workout it builds.

records.title: Show HN: go-git2 – 10-100x faster than go-git, libgit2 -> WASM -> Go
records.author: msuozzo
records.storyText:
go-git2 is a Go git library (read-only for now) using libgit2 transpiled to Go with wasm2go. As a result, it builds with CGO_ENABLED=0 and cross-compiles without a C toolchain. It supports 64-bit Linux, macOS, and Windows today.

While go-git has been great for my uses, its performance on larger repos and quirky differences from the git CLI output have been tricky to work with. I'm a huge fan of wasm2go and go-sqlite3 and wanted to apply the same approach and see what could be done. Incredibly happy with the results thus far, with 10-100x improvements on my real-world use cases. On the django repo, finding commits touching a file goes from 40s with go-git to 350ms, against 255ms for git itself. And the only unsafe is in wasm2go's bounds-checked memory accesses!

The API follows go-git v5, so read-only code is mostly a drop-in (still a few constructs to port). Write support is down the road.

The main module is MIT and the libgit2 module keeps the upstream license (GPLv2 w/ linking exception).

Give it a go!
